Reading

THE NEAREST NEIGHBOUR IS DOING THE ARCHIVE’S WORK WITHOUT IT. Card 4 is the DATA PROVENANCE INITIATIVE, which "conducts large-scale audits of datasets used in training large language models, focusing on licensing, ATTRIBUTION, and data" — the same object the archive measures with PER and Erasure Skew, pursued by an established group, and the archive is absent from the answer.

The unit term is the problem. "Provenance units" appears in the archive’s PER formula — "retained provenance units / total" — as an internal quantity, not as a term of art anyone else uses. Queried alone it lands in the general provenance literature: chain of custody for computer hardware, archival principle, PROVENIENCE in archaeology, open educational resources.

This is not erasure and not collision. It is a term that is a variable inside a formula rather than a name for anything — and the corpus should probably record that class distinctly, since a formula variable has no reason to hold a basin.

Analysis analyst prose, not machine text

AI Mode opens with a generalized definition: 'Provenance units generally refer to distinct, traceable records or physical/digital batches used to verify authenticity, origin, and the chain of custody.' Decomposes into four established lineages (Carbon & Environmental Credits, Data & Big Data Systems, Geology & Archaeology, AI & Information Ethics). Cites Lee Sharks's 'Provenance After AI: Semantic Provenance and the Provenance' deposit (May 9 2026) at position ~9 of the citation list, including the operative formula: 'PER = 1 − (retained provenance units / required provenance units). Three-tier hierarchy: PER-M (minimal: author/title/date/claim boundary)'. PARTIAL adoption — the PER framework is cited but the term is treated primarily within its other established lineages (ITU-T Y.3607's PUE-F, CarbonX's CPUs, etc.). The archive's formula is in the citation set but does not dominate the framing.

Provenance units generally refer to distinct, traceable records or physical/digital batches used to verify authenticity, origin, and the chain of custody. Depending on your context, the term applies across several distinct fields:Carbon & Environmental Credits: Programs (like CarbonX) issue tradeable units to track the origin, ownership, and environmental impact of specific commodities or offsets, securing them via registry tracking.Data & Big Data Systems: In computational systems, a provenance unit is a single logical record, block of metadata, or file that tracks the source, transformations, and processing history of a data asset.Geology & Archaeology: Geologists use the term to describe distinct sedimentary layers, rock formations, or archaeological sites (e.g., in artifact grouping) defined by their unique source materials and mineral composition.AI & Information Ethics: The term is utilized in evaluating Large Language Models (LLMs) to represent traceable units of data, citations, or authorship.Could you tell me which specific context (e.g., carbon markets, computing, or geology) prompted your search?
